name: how computational researchers audit and defend simulation credibility
goal: I am an undergraduate researcher producing a computational fluid dynamics style simulation result that will be defended in a paper and a poster, and I want to know how professional computational scientists actually audit work like mine before publishing it. My records are short, roughly ninety to three hundred output frames, and when I apply established equilibration and stationarity tests the effective sample size comes out between three and forty. I have found that a quantity I reported to five significant figures moved and changed sign when I simply reran at a longer record length, and that a ratio I was comparing against a published benchmark spans more than a factor of three across plausible choices of bed friction and grid resolution, with the flow regime itself changing as I refine the grid so that a grid convergence study is confounded. I want to know what the established practice is for reporting a discrete or classification outcome from a simulation whose underlying continuous quantities are not converged. I want to know how researchers handle the situation where the only available validation benchmark is at a completely different physical scale, three orders of magnitude apart in my case. Finally I want to know how negative and null results from simulation studies are reported credibly, because several of my own findings are refutations of my own earlier claims.
summary:
Credibility is a context-of-use claim built from separate evidence about code correctness, numerical solution accuracy, physical-model adequacy, and uncertainty, NOT a binary property conferred by agreement with one benchmark [Obe02b, Roy11, Mor19c].

DECISION-RELEVANT UNCERTAINTY.
- Richardson/GCI estimates are defensible only in an asymptotic refinement regime; NONMONOTONE OR NONCONVERGED RESULTS SHOULD BE TREATED AS NUMERICAL UNCERTAINTY, NOT REDUCED TO SPURIOUS SIGNIFICANT FIGURES [Roy10, Phi14, Log05].
- For a binary vehicle-movement verdict, THE USEFUL OBJECT IS THEREFORE A ROBUSTNESS OR FAILURE-PROBABILITY STATEMENT OVER RECORD LENGTH, FRICTION, RESOLUTION, AND MODEL ASSUMPTIONS. Threshold-based validation explicitly relates comparison error to DISTANCE FROM THE ENGINEERING THRESHOLD [Har17]. Correlated finite records must also carry sampling uncertainty [Oli12].
- A scale-mismatched benchmark supports only PARTIAL validation unless a hierarchy of simpler, shared-physics tests links it to the target; extrapolation uncertainty is a central unresolved problem [Oli14, Hil13, Rie20].

PARTICLE-METHOD EVIDENCE. No universal particle-method minimum has been adopted [Bra11]. A credible SPH case normally combines manufactured-solution/order tests, boundary-condition verification, conservation/stability checks, refinement studies, and validation of the coupled free-surface/solid physics [Neg21e, Neg22, Vac20]. Vehicle studies illustrate the value and limits of combining SPH with experiments [Azh23]; published stability thresholds themselves vary substantially across models and conditions [Boc19].

AUDITABILITY AND FAILURE MODES. Reproducibility requires versioned code, inputs, parameters, environment, hardware/parallel settings, workflow, and output provenance [Lei20b, Kra21, Dhr23]; CROSS-ARCHITECTURE AGREEMENT IS EVIDENCE OF ROBUSTNESS, NOT PHYSICAL VALIDITY, because rounding and parallel ordering can alter trajectories [Sen08, Gop21]. DOCUMENTED TRAPS INCLUDE AGREEMENT FOR THE WRONG REASONS [Ber18b] and underestimated iterative error [Eca20b]. NULL OR SELF-REFUTING RESULTS ARE STRONGEST WHEN REPORTED AS SENSITIVITY, UNCERTAINTY, AND DECISION-BOUNDARY FINDINGS RATHER THAN BURIED, consistent with validation being non-binary [Eas01].
